hello.title: Hello, Perl!
hello.summary: Write your first Perl programs with print and say, and start every program with use strict and use warnings.
hello.lesson.0: A program is a list of instructions for the computer. Perl runs them from top to bottom. You save a Perl program in a text file, for example `hello.pl`, and run it with the command `perl hello.pl`.
hello.lesson.1: Your first instruction is `print`: it writes text on the screen. Text between double quotes is called a **string**. Inside a string, `\n` means a line break. Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.
hello.lesson.3: The first two lines are not output. `use strict;` makes Perl stop at common mistakes, for example a misspelled variable name. `use warnings;` makes Perl print a warning when your code looks suspicious. Start every program with these two lines.
hello.lesson.4: `print` does not add a line break by itself. Without `\n`, the next `print` continues on the same line.
hello.lesson.7: `say` works like `print`, but it adds a line break at the end. You turn it on once with the line `use feature 'say';` at the top of the program. The rest of this course uses `say` in almost every program.
hello.lesson.9: `print` and `say` can show several values at once: separate them with commas. Numbers need no quotes, and Perl can calculate with `+`, `-`, `*` (multiply) and `/` (divide).
hello.lesson.11: Perl is case-sensitive: `say` works, `Say` does not. A `#` starts a comment: Perl ignores everything from `#` to the end of the line.
hello.lesson.12: A missing semicolon is the most common beginner mistake. Perl then reads two lines as one statement and stops with a `syntax error`.
hello.card.0: `use strict;` and `use warnings;` start every program
hello.card.1: `print "Hi\n";` prints text, `\n` is a line break
hello.card.3: `say "Hi";` prints text and a line break
hello-1.prompt: Which command runs the program in the file `hello.pl`?
hello-1.explain: You start a Perl program with the `perl` command, followed by the file name.
hello-2.explain: The first `print` has no line break, so the second `print` continues on the same line.
hello-3.explain: `say` prints the string and then the result of `4 * 5`, which is `20`.
hello-4.options.0: `AB` and then `C` on a new line
hello-4.options.3: `A` and then `BC` on a new line
hello-4.explain: `print "A"` adds no line break, so `B` follows directly. `\n` ends the line, and `say` prints `C` on the next line.
hello-5.statement: `say` adds a line break after the text, but `print` does not.
hello-5.explain: That is the only difference between the two. With `print`, you add `\n` yourself.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the line so that `say` works.
hello-6.explain: `use feature 'say';` turns on the `say` feature. The other words are not modules that turn on `say`.
hello-7.prompt: Build a line that prints `Sum: 7` and a line break.
hello-7.explain: `say` prints all values in the list and adds a line break. The comma separates the string from the calculation.
hello-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Perl is fun` and then `Bye`.
hello-8.explain: The three `print` lines build the first line, and `\n` ends it. Then `say` prints `Bye`.
hello-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-9.pairs.0: prints text without a line break
hello-9.pairs.1: prints text and a line break
hello-9.pairs.2: a line break inside a string
hello-10.explain: The statement has no semicolon at the end. Write `say "Line 1";`.
hello-11.explain: Perl is case-sensitive. The command is `print` in lowercase: `print "Middle\n";`.
hello-12.explain: Perl calculates `2 + 3` outside of quotes. Inside quotes, `2 + 3` is text, and `say "2", "3"` prints `23`.
scalars.title: Scalars
scalars.summary: Store numbers and strings in scalar variables, put them into strings and calculate with them.
scalars.lesson.0: A variable is a name for a value. In Perl, a variable that holds one value is called a **scalar**. Its name starts with `$`, for example `$name`. The value can be a number or a string. `my` creates a new variable, and `=` stores a value in it.
scalars.lesson.2: Inside double quotes, Perl replaces a variable with its value. This is called **interpolation**. Single quotes keep the text exactly as written: no variables and no `\n`.
scalars.lesson.5: Perl calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. `/` can give a decimal number. `%` gives the rest of a division, and `**` raises to a power. `$x += 3` is short for `$x = $x + 3`, and `$x++` adds 1.
scalars.lesson.8: The dot `.` joins two strings into one. The operator `x` repeats a string. `length` counts the characters of a string.
scalars.lesson.10: Perl changes between numbers and strings for you. The operator decides: `+` treats both values as numbers, `.` treats both values as strings. So `"3" + 4` is `7`, and `3 . 4` is `34`.
scalars.lesson.12: When letters follow a variable directly inside a string, put the name in braces: `"${fruit}s"` gives `apples` when `$fruit` is `"apple"`.
scalars.lesson.13: With `use strict`, you must create every variable with `my` before you use it. Otherwise Perl stops with the error `Global symbol "$total" requires explicit package name`.
scalars-1.explain: 17 divided by 5 is 3, with a rest of 2. `%` gives the rest.
scalars-3.explain: Single quotes do not interpolate, so Perl prints the text exactly as written, including `$item`.
scalars-4.explain: The dot `.` joins strings. Perl treats both values as strings, so the result is `53`.
scalars-5.statement: This program stops with an error.
scalars-5.explain: With `use strict`, every variable needs `my` the first time. Write `my $total = 5;`.
scalars-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Hello, Bob!`.
scalars-6.explain: The dot `.` joins strings. `+` and `*` calculate with numbers, and `x` repeats a string.
scalars-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `25`.
scalars-7.explain: `**` raises to a power: 5 to the power of 2 is 25. `5 * 2` is `10`, and `5 x 2` is the string `55`.
scalars-8.prompt: Build a line that creates the variable `$price` with the value `9.99`.
scalars-8.explain: `my` creates the variable, the name starts with `$`, and `=` stores the value. `==` compares, it does not store.
scalars-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Total: 12`.
scalars-9.explain: First create the variable. 2 + 4 is 6, and 6 * 2 is 12. Then print the result.
scalars-10.prompt: Match the operator with its meaning.
scalars-11.explain: `+` adds numbers. To join strings, use the dot: `my $full = $first . " " . $last;`.
scalars-12.explain: Single quotes do not interpolate, so this prints `$sum` as text. Use double quotes: `say "Sum: $sum";`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Run code only when a condition is true with if, elsif, else and unless, and compare numbers and strings.
conditions.lesson.0: `if` runs a block of code only when a condition is true. The condition goes in parentheses, and the block goes in braces `{ }`. Both are required. `elsif` checks another condition when the first one is false (note the spelling), and `else` runs when no condition was true. You compare numbers with `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`.
conditions.lesson.3: Perl has separate operators to compare strings: `eq` (equal), `ne` (not equal), `lt` (comes first in alphabetical order) and `gt` (comes later). Use `==` for numbers and `eq` for strings. The number `10` and the number `10.0` are equal, but the strings `"10"` and `"10.0"` are different.
conditions.lesson.5: If you compare strings with `==`, Perl turns them into numbers first. A word without digits becomes `0`, so `"abc" == "xyz"` is true. `use warnings` then prints a warning. Always use `eq` for strings.
conditions.lesson.7: Perl has no special values for true and false. The number `0`, the empty string `""`, the string `"0"` and an undefined value are false. Every other value is true. `unless` is the opposite of `if`: it runs the block when the condition is false.
conditions.lesson.9: You combine conditions with `&&` (and: both must be true) and `||` (or: at least one must be true). `!` (not) turns true into false and false into true.
conditions.lesson.11: For a single statement, you can put `if` or `unless` after it. This short form needs no parentheses and no braces.
conditions-1.explain: 15 is not greater than 20, but it is greater than 10, so the `elsif` block runs.
conditions-2.explain: The string `"0"` is false in Perl, so the `else` block runs.
conditions-3.prompt: Which operator checks if two strings are equal?
conditions-3.explain: `eq` compares strings. `==` compares numbers, and `=` stores a value.
conditions-4.explain: `==` turns both words into the number `0`, so the condition is true. `use warnings` reports that the strings are not numbers.
conditions-5.statement: In Perl, the keyword for "else if" is `elsif`.
conditions-5.explain: Perl writes `elsif`, without the second `e`. `else if` is a syntax error in Perl.
conditions-6.prompt: Complete the condition so that access needs both the right user and the right PIN.
conditions-6.explain: `&&` is true only when both conditions are true. Here the PIN is wrong, so access is denied. With `||`, the right user alone would be enough.
conditions-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Hello, Ada`.
conditions-7.explain: `eq` checks if two strings are equal. `ne` means not equal.
conditions-8.prompt: Build a line that prints `Adult` when `$age` is 18 or more.
conditions-8.explain: In the short form, the condition comes after the statement. `>=` means greater than or equal.
conditions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `5 is cold` and then `25 is warm`.
conditions-9.explain: The `if` runs inside the loop for each value. 5 is not greater than 20, so the `else` block runs. 25 is greater than 20.
conditions-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
conditions-10.pairs.4: runs when the condition is false
conditions-11.explain: Perl has no `else if`. Write `} elsif ($age >= 13) {`.
conditions-12.explain: `==` compares numbers, and both words become `0`. Compare strings with `eq`: `if ($answer eq "no") {`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with foreach, for and while, count with ranges like 1..5 and control loops with next and last.
loops.lesson.0: A loop repeats a block of code. `foreach` runs the block once for every value in a list. `1..4` is a **range**: the numbers from 1 to 4. The variable after `my` holds the current value in each round.
loops.lesson.2: `for` and `foreach` mean the same in Perl, and most people write the shorter `for`. A list can also be values in parentheses, separated by commas.
loops.lesson.5: `while` repeats the block as long as the condition is true. Change something inside the loop, otherwise it never ends. `$n *= 3` is short for `$n = $n * 3`.
loops.lesson.7: `for` also has a classic form with three parts, separated by semicolons: a start, a condition and a step that runs after each round. `$i -= 4` is short for `$i = $i - 4`.
loops.lesson.10: `next` jumps to the next round at once. `last` ends the loop at once. Both are often used with the short `if` form.
loops.lesson.12: A range always counts up, so `5..1` is an empty list. To count down, write `reverse 1..5`.
loops.card.2: `while ($n < 10) { }` repeats while the condition is true
loops.card.3: `next` jumps to the next round, `last` ends the loop
loops-1.explain: The loop adds 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. The sum is 15.
loops-2.explain: `$x` becomes 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. 32 is not less than 20, so the loop stops.
loops-3.prompt: How many lines does this print?
loops-3.explain: The range `3..7` contains 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7. That is five numbers.
loops-4.explain: `next` skips 3, and `last` ends the loop when `$i` is 5. So the loop prints 1, 2 and 4.
loops-5.explain: A range always counts up. `5..1` is an empty list, so the block never runs.
loops-6.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints 1, 2 and 3.
loops-6.explain: `1 .. 3` is the range 1, 2, 3. With a comma, the list has only 1 and 3.
loops-7.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints `1`, `2` and `3`.
loops-7.explain: `next` skips 4 and 9 and goes on with the next value. `last` would end the loop at the first value, 4.
loops-8.prompt: Build the first line of a loop that runs while `$count` is greater than `0`.
loops-8.explain: `while` repeats as long as the condition in parentheses is true.
loops-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Sum: 6`.
loops-9.explain: Create `$sum` before the loop, add inside the loop and print once after the loop.
loops-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
loops-10.pairs.3: repeats while a condition is true
loops-10.pairs.4: runs once for every value in a list
loops-11.explain: Perl is case-sensitive, and `$Total` was never created. Write `say "Total: $total";`.
loops-12.explain: Perl has no `stop`. To end a loop, write `last;`.
arrays.title: Arrays
arrays.summary: Keep many values in order in an array, add and remove items with push and pop, and use join and sort.
arrays.lesson.0: An **array** stores a list of scalars in a fixed order. Its name starts with `@`. You create it with a list in parentheses. Inside double quotes, an array prints its items with a space between them.
arrays.lesson.2: Each item has an **index**, a position number that starts at `0`. One item is a scalar, so you write `$fruits[0]` with `$`, not `@`. A negative index counts from the end: `$fruits[-1]` is the last item.
arrays.lesson.3: `push` adds items at the end of an array. `pop` removes the last item and returns it, so you can store it in a variable.
arrays.lesson.5: You change an item with `=`. `scalar(@colors)` gives the number of items, and `$#colors` gives the last index.
arrays.lesson.7: `foreach` goes through the items of an array, one after the other.
arrays.lesson.10: `join` glues all items into one string, with a separator between them. `sort` returns a sorted copy of a list. By default, it sorts alphabetically.
arrays.lesson.12: `sort` compares strings by default, so `10` comes before `9`. To sort numbers, write `sort { $a <=> $b } @nums`. `$a` and `$b` are special variables that `sort` fills with two items, and `<=>` compares them as numbers.
arrays.card.1: `$list[0]` is the first item, `$list[-1]` the last
arrays-1.explain: Indexes start at 0, so index 2 is the third item.
arrays-2.explain: The array has three items, and `push` adds a fourth.
arrays-3.explain: The index `-1` means the last item.
arrays-4.explain: Without a block, `sort` compares strings character by character. `"1"` comes before `"2"`, and `"2"` before `"3"`.
arrays-5.statement: `pop` removes the first item of an array.
arrays-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `red green blue`.
arrays-6.explain: `push` adds `"blue"` at the end of the array.
arrays-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `1, 2, 3`.
arrays-7.explain: `join` puts the separator `", "` between the items and returns one string.
arrays-8.prompt: Build a line that creates the array `@pets`, so that `say "@pets";` prints `cat dog`.
arrays-8.explain: An array name starts with `@`, and the items go in parentheses, separated by commas.
arrays-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `3 5 7`.
arrays-9.explain: Create the array, add 5, sort the numbers and then print them.
arrays-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
arrays-10.pairs.0: adds an item at the end
arrays-11.explain: Indexes start at 0. The first item is `$animals[0]`.
arrays-12.explain: `sort` without a block compares strings, so `12` comes first. Sort numbers with `my @sorted = sort { $a <=> $b } @nums;`.
hashes.title: Hashes
hashes.summary: Store pairs of keys and values in a hash, check keys with exists and loop over a hash in a fixed order.
hashes.lesson.0: A **hash** stores pairs of keys and values. You look up a value by its key, like a word in a dictionary. A hash name starts with `%`. Between a key and its value you write `=>`.
hashes.lesson.2: One value is a scalar, so you read it with `$` and the key in braces: `$ages{"Ann"}`. When the key is a simple word, you can leave out the quotes.
hashes.lesson.3: You add a new pair or change a value with `=`.
hashes.lesson.5: `exists` checks whether a key is in the hash. `delete` removes a key and its value.
hashes.lesson.8: `keys %price` gives a list of all keys, and `values %price` a list of all values. A hash has no fixed order, and the order can change every time the program runs. For a fixed order, sort the keys: `sort keys %price`.
hashes.lesson.10: `scalar(keys %points)` counts the pairs. When the order does not matter, for example for a sum, you can use `values` directly.
hashes.lesson.12: A hash is great for counting. `my %count;` creates an empty hash. `$count{$w}++` adds 1 to the value of the key `$w`. A new key starts at 0.
hashes.card.1: `$h{Ann}` reads a value, `$h{Cy} = 40;` adds a pair
hashes.card.3: `for my $k (sort keys %h) { }` loops in a fixed order
hashes.card.4: `values %h` gives the values, `scalar(keys %h)` counts the pairs
hashes-1.explain: `$color{grass}` reads the value of the key `grass`.
hashes-2.explain: `$h{c} = 3` adds a new key, but `$h{a} = 10` only changes an existing value. So there are three keys.
hashes-3.explain: `exists` only checks if the key is there. The value `0` does not matter.
hashes-4.explain: `sort keys` returns the keys in alphabetical order.
hashes-5.statement: `keys %h` always returns the keys in the order you added them.
hashes-5.explain: A hash has no fixed order. Use `sort keys %h` when you need a fixed order.
hashes-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Paris`.
hashes-6.explain: One value of a hash is a scalar, so you write `$` before the name: `$capital{France}`.
hashes-7.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints the pairs in alphabetical order of the keys.
hashes-7.explain: `sort keys %h` returns the keys in alphabetical order.
hashes-8.prompt: Build a line that adds the key `"Eve"` with the value `28` to the hash `%ages`.
hashes-8.explain: One value is a scalar, so the line starts with `$ages`. The key goes in braces, and `=` stores the value.
hashes-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `a: 2`.
hashes-9.explain: Create the empty hash first, count every word in the loop and print the result after the loop.
hashes-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hashes-10.pairs.1: the value of the key k
hashes-10.pairs.4: checks if the key is there
hashes-11.explain: `$ages{name}` looks up the key `"name"`. Use the variable: `say "$name is $ages{$name}";`.
hashes-12.explain: `keys` gives the names `tea` and `cake`, not the prices. Use `for my $p (values %price) {`.
subs.title: Subroutines
subs.summary: Put code into reusable subroutines, pass arguments with @_ and give back results with return.
subs.lesson.0: A **subroutine**, or sub, is a named block of code that you can run many times. You define it with `sub`, a name and a block in braces. You run, or **call**, it with its name and parentheses.
subs.lesson.2: The values in the parentheses of a call are the **arguments**. Inside the sub, they are in the special array `@_`. `my ($name) = @_;` copies the first argument into a new variable. A variable created with `my` inside a sub exists only inside that sub.
subs.lesson.4: `return` gives a value back to the caller. You can store the result in a variable or use it directly.
subs.lesson.6: Do not forget the parentheses in `my ($name) = @_;`. Without them, `my $count = @_;` stores the number of arguments, because an array used as a single value gives its size.
subs.lesson.8: `return` also ends the sub at once. This works well with the short `if` form.
subs.lesson.10: A sub can take any number of arguments. When you pass an array, all its items go into `@_`.
subs.lesson.12: A sub can also return a list. You catch the values with a list of variables in parentheses.
subs.card.0: `sub name { ... }` defines a sub, `name();` calls it
subs.card.3: `my` variables in a sub exist only inside it
subs-3.explain: Without parentheses, `my $n = @_;` stores the number of arguments, which is 3.
subs-4.explain: 15 is greater than 10, so the first call returns `big`. For 5, the first `return` is skipped and the sub returns `small`.
subs-5.explain: `$level` is created with `my` inside the sub, so it does not exist outside it. With `use strict`, Perl stops with an error.
subs-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Hi, Sam`.
subs-6.explain: The arguments of a sub are in the array `@_`.
subs-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `9`.
subs-7.explain: `return` gives the value back, and the `say` outside prints it. A `say` inside the sub would print an extra line.
subs-8.prompt: Build a line that calls `diff` with the arguments `10` and `4`, in this order, and stores the result in a new variable `$result`.
subs-8.explain: The arguments go in parentheses after the name of the sub. `my` creates the new variable.
subs-9.prompt: Put the lines in order to define a sub that returns the largest number.
subs-9.explain: Copy the arguments, sort them as numbers and return the last item, which is the largest.
subs-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
subs-10.pairs.4: calls a sub with two arguments
subs-11.explain: Without parentheses, `$name` gets the number of arguments. Write `my ($name) = @_;`.
subs-12.explain: When `$x` is not greater, the larger number is `$y`. The line must be `return $y;`.
regex.title: Regular expressions
regex.summary: Search text with patterns using =~ and m//, capture parts of a match and replace text with s///.
regex.lesson.0: A **regular expression**, or regex, is a pattern that describes text. `=~` applies a pattern to a string. `m/Perl/`, or short `/Perl/`, is true when the text contains `Perl` anywhere. `!~` is true when the text does not match.
regex.lesson.2: In a pattern, `^` means the start of the string and `$` means the end. The letter `i` after the pattern ignores the difference between upper and lower case.
regex.lesson.4: Some characters have a special meaning. `\d` matches one digit, `\w` one letter, digit or `_`, and `\s` one space. A dot `.` matches any character, so write `\.` for a real dot. `+` after a character means one or more times, and `*` means zero or more times.
regex.lesson.7: Parentheses in a pattern **capture** the part of the text they match. After a successful match, the first group is in `$1`, the second in `$2`, and so on. You can also assign the captured groups to a list of variables.
regex.lesson.10: `s/old/new/` replaces the first match in a variable. The variable itself changes. With `g` at the end, it replaces every match.
regex.lesson.12: The new text can use the captured groups. `s///` also returns the number of replacements.
regex.card.1: `^` start, `$` end, `\d` digit, `\w` word character, `+` one or more
regex-1.explain: `\d+` finds the first group of digits, `42`, and the parentheses capture it into `$1`.
regex-2.explain: `\.` matches a real dot, and `g` replaces every dot with `-`.
regex-3.explain: The pattern allows only digits from the start `^` to the end `$`. The other strings contain a space, letters or `!`.
regex-4.explain: Without `g`, `s///` replaces only the first match.
regex-5.explain: Patterns are case-sensitive: `world` does not match `World`. With `/world/i`, it would match.
regex-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `yes`.
regex-6.explain: The `i` after the pattern ignores upper and lower case.
regex-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `2024`.
regex-7.explain: The pattern has one group, so the captured digits are in `$1`.
regex-8.prompt: Build a line that replaces every `x` in `$word` with `y`.
regex-8.explain: `=~` applies `s///` to `$word`, and `g` replaces every match, not only the first.
regex-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Hello, Ada`.
regex-9.explain: First replace `: ` with `=`. Then the pattern matches and captures `Ada` into `$name`.
regex-10.prompt: Match the pattern part with its meaning.
regex-10.pairs.4: applies a pattern to a string
regex-11.explain: The second group is in `$2`. Write `say "Number: $2";`.
regex-12.explain: `=` stores the result of `s///` instead of changing `$text`. Use `=~`: `$text =~ s/one/1/g;`.
